content.comment:
Hi, thanks for your work on out-of-distribution detection. The authors propose to use cosine similarity, as the calculation in last layer instead of matrix multiplication, to train the model together with the predicted temperature scaling which is utilizing batch normalization followed by Sigmoid function. The performance is further improved by the input processing using only in-distribution to search for the appropriate \epsilon. In addition, authors also provide the analysis on the robustness of proposed method, and show the results on the experiment on domain shifting datasets.

These are my questions:
1. In section 3.1, there exists the explanation about the theory behind this method. Authors explain that $g(x)$ is used in order to represent the distribution of $p(d_{in}|x)$. If this is true, why is not this value, $g(x)$, used as the measurement for detect the OOD samples? Why $h(x)$ is used, and what does the $h(x)$ term represent in the equation?
2. The authors mentioned previous work, Mahalanobis OOD detector (Lee et. al. 2018b) which introduced the idea to detect the OOD samples by only using the adversarial image that is created from in-distribution dataset, and the concurrent work Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) which also proposed the idea to detect the OOD samples without having the access to the explicit OOD dataset. Why do the authors claim “To our knowledge, this is the first study focused on such a minimal setting, investigating the feasibility of learning out-of-distribution detection without out-of-distribution data”?
3. Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) also utilizes the cosine similarity and predicted temperature scale for the predictions. Further, this cited paper also remove the effect of the weight regularization in the last layer. Authors claim that cited paper is a specific way to instantiate authors’ framework, but in fact the best measurement in authors’ framework utilize the same calculation with them, which is cosine similarity. The input processing is a slightly modified version from the method proposed by Liang et. al. 2017. The authors compose several techniques which are already known. So, what is the clear contribution of this paper?
4. The authors show the performance of proposed method compared to the several previous work. Previous works tend to show the result from more than one network architectures. Why authors only show the performance of DenseNet in the main part?
With kind regards,
content.title: Questions about the paper

replying_to: Replying to Questions about the paper

content.comment: Thanks for your interest in our work. It is our pleasure to answer your questions. First of all, we notice that your summarization stressed the view of model implementation, instead of the ideas that lead to such an implementation. Therefore please allow us to balance such a view at the beginning since one of the focus in our work is on a more unified, general idea of how overconfidence can be decomposed. Our results show that the effect of decomposition can be achieved in multiple ways. Thus we view those design choices (e.g., using inner-product, Euclidean distance, or cosine similarity) as the support for the idea instead of a canonical implementation. We are aware that one of our variants, which uses cosine similarity, is similar to the wonderful concurrent work done by Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) on arXiv (cited in our paper), and we are excited to see that. When a model can be explained from two different views (Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) is from metric learning while ours is from decomposed confidence), it is a good indication that this line of ideas is worth more attention and discussions from the community. Your specific questions are answered in the next text box due to the character limit.
content.title: Responses

content.comment:
1. We use h(x) to relate to the term p(y,d|x) while g(x) relates to p(d|x). Both can be used for OOD detection, and the selection is part of the design choice. We select h(x) for further analysis since its coupling with class prediction naturally leads to several simple design choices (e.g., inner-product, Euclidean distance, cosine similarity) for a comparison. Empirically we found g(x) can work as well as h(x) when the in-distribution dataset is simple (e.g., CIFAR-10) but worse when the dataset is harder (e.g., CIFAR-100). Such a trend of the robustness of g(x) is similar to the h(x) implemented with the inner-product, which might be because of the use of the inner-product in g(x) as well. Further, in the case of noisy or imperfect estimates (which will be the case for more complex datasets) incorporating the joint probability estimate of the class label and in-distribution probability can be more robust; specifically, h(x) always has the chance to learn to estimate p(y|x) when p(y,d|x) is hard to learn, but g(x) has no such fallback option and thus must resort to providing a flatter distribution. In other words, h(x) works at least as good as the “Plain” (see Figure 1(a)) while g(x) is not. We will supplement the results of using g(x) in an updated appendix.

2. The difference in problem setting validates our claim regarding our novel setting with respect to the two referred works, elaborated below. First, the Mahalanobis paper (Lee et. al. 2018b) described an alternative strategy for collecting OOD data, which is to generate it instead of using real OOD data. However, it does not eliminate the need of having OOD data from the algorithm, and the design of the generation process (including the choice of hyperparameters for the generation) could still bias the algorithm. In contrast, our work targets a setting that avoids using OOD data in any form. Second, the work done by Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) focuses on a setting which avoids hyperparameter tuning. Although it implies not using OOD data, It is a stricter setting than ours since we allow hyperparameter tuning with in-distribution data. In summary, the two mentioned works do not fully match our setting of learning without OOD data; therefore the space of potential methods for the problem is different. 

3. We do not agree with the comment “The authors compose several techniques which are already known”. First, the concept of decomposed confidence has not been discussed in previous literature and adds significant justification and insight that did not exist before. Although one of its variants (which uses cosine similarity) leads to a similar model used by Techapanurak & Okatani (2019), such a result is reached through different paths (Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) is from metric learning while ours is from decomposed confidence). Furthermore, our results show that cosine similarity works great, but it is not the top performer in all cases. For example, Figure 1a shows that the Euclidean distance performs slightly better than cosine similarity. We show the results with cosine similarity more often in the main paper because it demonstrates better robustness in our analysis (Figure 3), while we leave the full results in appendix Table 5 and 6. Second, we modify the input preprocessing strategy, so it does not require OOD data. This modification makes a significant change in the paradigm and is not seen in previous literature. Lastly, our analysis with different types of distribution shifts (semantic and non-semantic) with a larger scale real-world images points out what is a more difficult scenario for the OOD detection. Such an analysis has not been seen in previous literature as well. In summary, our decomposed confidence, modified input preprocessing, and the comprehensive analysis form the major contributions to the OOD detection problem.

4. Our submission has the experiments with all types of networks used in the previous OOD detection paper. We include DenseNet, WRN, and ResNet with varied depth. The results are summarized in Figure 4. We put DenseNet results in Table 1 because most of the previous OOD papers have DenseNet results, so we align such practice for readers to compare across papers easily.
content.title: (continue)

display_title: Questions regards to the authors' reply

content.comment:
Thanks for the authors' reply. These are my questions regards to the authors' reply.

1. The claim that $h(x)$ represents $p(y, d_in|x)$ is interesting. But
1.1)  there is a controversy for the claim "$g(x)$ relates to $p(d_in|x)$". Could the authors share about how likely the value of this term is adjusted? Due to mathematical intuition studied in previous works, this term is adjusted to be near zero for all samples, both training & test dataset, and for those all of OOD datasets, at the end of the training. This phenomena exists especially for the case of CIFAR-100 where the amount of the target class is high. Does this situation exist in the authors' experiments as well? If so, what is the intuition why does this term, $p(d_in|x)$, approach to the low value even in definite in-distribution, training samples?
1.2) The authors mentioned that the term $g(x)$ could not be an efficient measurement for OOD detection since the calculation is the inner-product. Is there any support for this claim?
1.3) What is the purpose for showing the classification performance of plain cosine? The inability of this network setting has already been raised in previous works. This plot might lead to misunderstanding that the improvement is from DeConf, which is wrong.

2. About the previous work, Lee et. al. 2018b proposed the alternative way to use the generated adversarial samples as the dataset for choosing their hyperparameters. I agree that there remains a hyperparameter in the adversarial generation. But for Techapanurak & Okatani (2019), the authors mentioned in the above reply, “Although it implies not using OOD data, It is a stricter setting than ours since we allow hyperparameter tuning with in-distribution data.”, means that the claim “To our knowledge, this is the first study focused on such a minimal setting, investigating the feasibility of learning out-of-distribution detection without out-of-distribution data” is not valid. Is this correct?

3. Due to the question 1.1 the concept of decomposed confidence would be the authors’ contribution if and only if the explanation of $g(x)$ is true. But, it is still unclear. The contribution of the authors are that the authors provide the generic way to justify the work of Techapanurak & Okatani (2019), and the authors propose the input processing without the explicit OOD sample which is amazing. Is it worth mentioning “previous work” rather than “concurrent work”? However, does input processing improve the AUROC in all cases? If not, how many cases are improved?

4. In table 2, the authors present that proposed method outperforms even when the other methods use the explicit OOD samples. This is a good point to show. But, readers should be noticed that this superiority is not consistent in every case. It works especially well with the DenseNet as backbone. In the supplementary part, the proposed method on Resent-34 does not outperform the reported performance in $Maha_{orig}$.

With kind regards,

content.title: Responses
content.comment:
Thanks for raising further discussions.
1. First of all, the injection of the structure does not guarantee h(x) behaves like p(y,d|x), and g(x) behaves like p(d|x), but there might be such a tendency when the structure is imposed. We therefore explore a set of simple choices for h(x) and g(x) to show the decomposed confidence property can emerge easily, demonstrating such prior knowledge (Eq. 4) is useful for the problem. 
(1.1) The g(x) predicts different values for different inputs, and its range of values also depends on the choice of h(x). For example, the cosine similarity has a numerical range between -1 and 1 (which is a smaller range compared to others, such as Euclidean distance) thus its associated g(x) tend to give a smaller value so that f(x) is able to minimize the cross-entropy further. Empirically, we see g(x) outputs values around 0.4(+-0.1) for in-distribution data (CIFAR-10), while outputting 0.1(+-0.09) for the OOD data (random noise) when the h(x) uses Euclidean distance. In comparison, the values from g(x) are around 0.009(+-0.001) with in-distribution data and 0.006(+-0.0001) with OOD data when h(x) uses cosine similarity.
Second, the question in the last sentence is not clear. In general, the p(d_in|x) is expected to have a larger value for the in-distribution data compared to the out-of-distribution data, and empirically g(x) does output such a trend (described above) with a simple dataset (CIFAR-10). When the dataset is harder (CIFAR-100), both in-distribution and out-of-distribution data lead to similar g(x) values (e.g., 0.003+-0.0002 when h(x) uses cosine similarity), which is smaller than CIFAR-10 cases mentioned above.
(1.2) As we mentioned in (1.1) and in the previous response, we observe that the g(x) implemented with the inner-product works well on a simple dataset but not on a harder one. We have those results and will add them to an updated appendix. Please note that the update is only allowed in a later stage of the review process.
(1.3) This question asks about the Figure 1b, which investigates the impact of DeConf for the classification accuracy of in-domain data. The primary conclusion extracted from Figure 1b is that the DeConf has a small negative impact on the accuracy compared to a vanilla classification network. We do not see anything “wrong” in the way Figure 1b is interpreted. Further, we have all combinations of settings in Figure 1b and let the results speak for themselves. It is good to see cosine similarity works with the DeConf while plain cosine similarity had a hard time on that case. That shows the DeConf can accommodate the h(x) of varied characteristics.

2. We do not agree with that view. As the difference mentioned in the previous response, the concurrent work of Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) has a stricter setting than ours, which leads to a significant difference in the space of potential methods for the problem.

3. Our contribution has been elaborated on in our previous response. Regarding the questions: First, the two works appear to be delivered at a similar time; thus we cite it as a concurrent work. If the work of Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) has been accepted by a venue, please kindly let us know, and we would be happy to update it. Second, for the question about the performance of modified input preprocessing, its results are summarized in Figure 2. 

4. Yes and we do use a conservative word for describing that results in our “contribution” paragraph: “The results show that the two strategies can significantly improve upon baseline methods, achieving a performance close to, and in several cases surpassing, state-of-the-art methods (Lee et al., 2018b) which use out-of-distribution data for tuning.”

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
- Summary: This paper proposes to train an OOD detection model without OOD data, because OOD is hard to define a-priori, such that OOD observed during training is not guaranteed to be matched with OOD at test time. They propose a decomposed confidence strategy and modification on input preprocessing. They show the superiority of their method over the state-of-the-art methods, when OOD is not available.


- Decision and supporting arguments:
Weak reject.

1. The analysis around `g` is confusing. After equation 5, they state that "`g(x)` is shared among all classes like p(d_in|x)." At this point, I expect that `g` is a confidence score, but at last they used `max_i h_i` for OOD detection, and the role of `g` turned out to be just a learnable temperature in softmax. Also, even the learning objective for `g` is not introduced. Also, it seems the authors tried to make some relationship between equation 4 and their method, but I couldn't find their correlation.

2. Contribution is limited. To my understand, the main novelty in this paper is on the learnable temperature `g`, and the others are already explored in the literature. The proposed three similarity measures are used in prior works, i.e., inner-product in Hendrycks & Gimpel (2017), Euclidean distance in Lee et al. (2018b) (though they claimed that Mahalanobis distance is better), and Cosine similarity in Techapanurak & Okatani (2019).
The essential modification on input preprocessing strategy is simply removing OOD data from the validation set, and this is a natural setting as their proposal is to train an OOD detection model without OOD data.


- Comments:
1. How is `g` trained? What is the learning objective and how the ground truth value is assigned? Since the activation of `g` is sigmoid, a natural conjecture is that in-distribution and OOD would be labeled as 1 and 0 (or reversed). However, they said they do not train their model with any OOD, so it is hard to figure out the learning objective and the ground truth value for `g`.

2. Why don't you compare with the GAN-based OOD generation (Lee et al., 2018a) and the adversarial attack-based validation (Lee et al., 2018b)? They do not require any OOD as well. In section 2.1, the authors set the hyperparameter `alpha_l` in the Mahalanobis method to be uniform because no OOD for validation is available, but actually Lee et al. (2018b) proposed the adversarial attack-based validation method to avoid the dependency on OOD.

3. Notation is confusing. `f` is used for multiple parts: `f_i = h_i/g` in eq 5 and `h` is a function of `f^p`. Some notations like `w_g` and `b_g` are not defined.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
Summary: This paper proposes a method for detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) data. Unlike most methods in this direction, this paper considers the scenario where a sample of out-of-distribution is not observed. Thus, the goal is detecting the out-of-distribution data using solely in-of-distribution data. First, the authors proposed to use input preprocessing similarly to ODIN (Liang et al., 2017) but the proposed scheme does not require out-of-distribution data. The way to search a parameter is different from the existing work (Liang et al., 2017). The proposed scheme looks simple and highly effective in the experiments. They also propose to decompose the learned function $f_i(x)$ into two parts for making a good confidence score function. Finally, they illustrate a good performance on OOD detection using their proposed methods (combining the decomposition and preprocessing).

========================================================
Clarity:
Overall, I found this paper is well-written and easy to follow. Only Section 3.1 highly concerns me on the clarity and correctness of the paper.

The part that I am most concern about is the decomposed confidence, I am not sure that the argument of the proposed method about confidence decomposition is correct. If the authors can convince me that it is correct, I will consider improving the score.
========================================================
Comments:

On the claim of the novelty of the problem setting:
This paper claims that this paper is the first study focused on a minimal setting, where I think it means the setting that we do not assume that we have OOD sample when training a model. However, there already are existing works on this issue. And it is more important to discuss them in the Related Methods section (2.1) rather than mentioning the most related works as the work that requires true OOD sample when training. I read the discussion in the comment section on how the authors tried to state the reason why they think it is novel, but I think it is not sufficient. It is the freedom to choose how to solve this problem, e.g., one may try to construct pseudo-OOD data from in-distribution data. But the core setting is the same, that is, OOD detection without OOD data. The authors may instead criticize that the method that generates pseudo-OOD from in-distribution may be unreliable, biased, and that's why other methods perform better. For the discussion about Hyperparameter-free, to me, it is simply a unique feature that Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) wanted to highlight as a contribution. Thus, the author may suggest a way to criticize that paper, e.g., it's better to tune so we can do well on the dataset we are interested in instead of saying that hyperparameter-free makes the setting different. Not only these two works I mentioned, I believe OOD detection itself has a long history and I do not think it is important to state that this paper is the first one to consider such a setting. 

On the confidence decomposition Section (3.1):

On why the network is overconfident:
In 3.1, the authors attempted to illustrate why neural networks may give an overconfident value for OOD data. I strongly agree that it is an important problem to discuss. In the example in 3.1, it is understandable that in Eq. (4), both values of numerator and denominator can be low when using OOD data. However, from my viewpoint, Eq. (4) suggests that in practice, the left-hand side of Eq. (4) can be unstable when x comes from OOD data (since the denominator can be very small, so as the numerator). And we do not have much data in that region, which makes p(y|x) estimation difficult in that region. From this logic, I think this equation does not only suggests overconfident but also it can tend to be underconfident too, especially in the semantic shift scenario. Thus this Eq. (4) does not suggest that the network tends to be overconfident but tend to have an extreme value (please correct me if I misunderstood). Therefore, it would be better to focus on discussing this issue of stability rather than giving a bit ad-hoc example 0.09/0.1 = 0.9 (overconfident). Although underconfidence can be easily handled because those data are easy to detect them as out-of-distribution.

On the influence of Eq. (4) to inspire $f_i(x) = \frac{h_i(x)}{g(x)}$:
I cannot see how $g(x)$ will relate to the denominator of Eq. (4). It is true that $g(x)$ is a function that is not class-specific, similarly to the denominator of Eq. (4). However, the denominator in Eq. (4) is just simply marginalized y out by taking a summation of all class-specific function. Thus, I think the only way to relate Eq. (4) to Eq. (5) is $\sum_{j=1}^C \exp f_j(x)$ is the unnormalized version of the denominator of Eq. (4), while $\frac{h_i(x)}{g(x)}$ is an unnormalized version of the numerator. Thus, I am not convince that Eq. (4) motivates $f_i(x) = \frac{h_i(x)}{g(x)}$.


On the input preprocessing Section (3.2):
I found the method for selecting the perturbation magnitude is very interesting and this is the most thing I like about this paper. It made me convinced that input preprocessing is highly useful and impactful for tacking OOD detection without OOD data (while ODIN already suggested this fact in the context where we have OOD sample). It enhances the performance of almost all cases as we can see from Figure 2. I have a positive impression on this part. It would be nice to see the performance of Deconf-C, which is almost identical to Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) in Table 1 to highlight the improvement from this preprocessing for different OOD datasets instead of averaging them all (as Figure 2). I think it is not too difficult to modify this part to highlight a contribution of the preprocessing part (currently only Figure 2 highlights the usefulness of it).

On experiments: 
It is also important to see a standard deviation of the results. Especially if we only run only a few times (three times in this context). If the standard deviation is high, it is highly suggested to run more times to get a reliable result. In addition, we may use a better criterion to bold a score (e.g., one-sided t-test). I also would like to know if the existing method has a higher standard deviation due to less stability when g(x) is not 1 or a constant (T) as they were in most existing approaches. Other than this point, I think the authors did a great job to visualize and show the effectiveness of decomposing a confidence score and the advantage of input preprocessing. Experiments on semantic/non-semantic shift is also interesting.
========================================================
Decision:
Although this paper proposed an interesting simple yet effective way to preprocess the data combining with decomposing a confidence function into two parts, I feel that the discussion of the relationship with existing methods and the clarification of the novelty have to be improved. Also, I disagree with the explanation of decomposed confidence part, and it simply looks like a scaling factor that depends on x to me.  Finally, reviewers are suggested to put a higher standard for evaluation for a paper more than 9 pages. For these reasons, in the current form, I vote to reject for this paper. If I am convinced that the discussion about decomposed confidence is valid, I will consider improving the score.
========================================================
Minor comments:
1. Does \log between gradient and S exist in Eq. (7) like the paper by Liang et al., 2017 ?
2. typo: Section 4.3: We therfore -> We therefore
========================================================
On the similar work by Techapanurak & Okatani (2019):
I am aware that the two works are concurrent and I still treat this part as the authors' contribution in my evaluation.

In my view, both works are are highly related.  I am aware that the work by Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) is also very recent (25 May 2019: arXiv) and the authors suggested it to be a concurrent work. It is also nice and I appreciate that the authors cited them. But since the authors discussed a little bit about their work, I think it is fruitful to discuss them in detail and point out the difference clearly, for example in the related work section. 

Here are four reasons I think why they are highly related. 
 
1. Same setting: OOD detection without OOD data

2. The authors attempted to clarify the difference and pointed out that the proposed framework is more general than Techapanurak & Okatani (2019). However, in my view, Techapanurak & Okatani also proposed to decompose the function into two parts, where $s$ (or $s(x)$) in Eq. (3) of Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) is strictly the same as $\frac{1}{g(x)}$ in this submitted work. Even before Techapanurak & Okatani (2019), people have been using this scaling parameter to improve the class posterior estimation (perhaps s = 1/T is the most common, although it does not depend on x). For the numerator $h_i(x)$, Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) proposed to change the standard $h_i^I(x)$ to $h_i^C(x)$. Although they did not write clearly that $h_i^I(x)$ can be something other than $h_i^C(x)$, the fact that they changed it is straightforward to see that we are able to generalize it and try other $h_i^I(x)$. Thus, the novelty of the generalization of Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) that this paper suggests is modest. 

3. The choice of $g(x)$ in this paper and $s(x)$ in Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) are almost identical. It is very slightly different in my view (not sure if it changes the performance). In this context, if I understand correctly, Techapanurak & Okatani (2019) used $g(x) = \frac{1}{exp(BN(linear-transformation))}$ while this paper proposed $\frac{1}{(1+exp(-BN(linear-transformation))}$.

4. The $h_i(x)$ that works best is the $h_i^C(x)$ proposed by Techapanurak & Okatani (2019).

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
Summary:  Inspired by recent methods that aim to make neural networks (NNs) robust by training on both in- and out-of-distribution (OOD) data [Liang et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2018], this paper addresses the question of if the same level of robustness can be obtained without training on an OOD set.  The authors propose introducing an auxiliary variable $d_{\text{in}}$ to directly model whether a given input originates from the training data or not.  Of course, training a function to predict $d_{\text{in}}$ directly would require OOD data or at least a simulation of OOD from in-distribution data.  To bypass this obstacle, the authors make an argument that parametrizing the softmax input with two functions---$f_{c}(x) = h_{c}(x)/g(x)$---is reminiscent of computing the conditional probability $p(y|d_{\text{in}}, x) = p(y, d_{\text{in}} | x) / p(d_{\text{in}}| x)$, with $h$ representing the joint density and $g$ the marginal.  The paper also proposes an input perturbation strategy similar to Liang et al.’s [2017], the difference being the perturbation magnitude is set by maximizing $h$ instead of on OOD data.  Experiments are reported showing performance on OOD detection, OOD detection when having access to OOD data during training vs when not, the effect of different choices of $h$, the effect of the proposed data augmentation strategy, the effect of number of samples, classes, and architecture parameters, and the effect of the distributional shifts being semantic vs non-semantic.       

Pros:  Making deep learning methods robust to distributional shift is essential for their safe deployment.  As the paper notes, many previously proposed methodologies require access to OOD data.  However, this reliance on OOD data not only adds implementation costs (extra memory and computation) but also makes the choice of OOD set a crucial modeling decision.  I am unaware of any rigorous guidance for selecting a representative OOD set for a given training set.  This paper makes some incremental but important contributions in relieving ODIN of its dependence on OOD data.  These proposals are supported with a fairly thorough experimental investigation.  The paper reports not only comparisons against sensible baselines but also performs ablation studies to isolate the effect of parametrization choices and their data augmentation strategy.    

Cons:  My most significant critique of the paper is that it exaggerates its contributions and ignores a large body of previous work.  There are two falsely claimed contributions in particular.  The first is that the paper is the first to consider OOD detection without training with OOD data: “To our knowledge, this is the first study focused on such a minimal setting, investigating the feasibility of learning out-of-distribution detection without out-of-distribution data” (p 2).  This is patently false.  Classification with a rejection option has been studied for many years, and much of this work does not assume access to an OOD set.  For just one example, Hellman [1970] considers k-nearest neighbor classification with a rejection option and requires no OOD set.  Perhaps the authors meant this as a contribution w.r.t. neural networks, but that is not the case either.  Cordella et al. [1995] studied rejection rules for MLPs, and Geifman & El-Yaniv [2017] studied selective classification for deep networks.  To the best of my knowledge, neither of these works require OOD data for training (although I am not intimately familiar with the methodology). 

The second falsely claimed contribution is the use of an auxiliary variable to represent that the data is in-distribution: “We specifically add a binary variable, representing whether the data is in-distribution or not” (p 2).  It surprises me that the authors would think that this idea hadn’t been proposed before, given its a rather obvious thing to try.  The idea dates back at least to Cortes et al. [2016]; see Section 2.1 on “General Rejection Models.”  Geifman & El-Yaniv [2017] use the same framework in the deep learning setting, defining a binary “selection function.”  Given these omissions, the paper cannot be accepted in its current form.  It requires substantial revisions: discussion of this previous work and modification of the claimed contributions.  I think a proper characterization of the work would to be to call it an extension of ODIN: using a selection function to parametrize ODIN’s temperature.  

Yet this brings another question to the forefront: why is $h(x)$ used to determine rejection when $g(x)$ is supposed to be a proxy for $p(d_{\text{in}} | x)$ (Equation 4)?  In the public discussion, the authors state that $g(x)$ does indeed work to a degree, but just not as well.  This seems to call into question the foundational motivations of the procedure, and the authors should address this by including experiments comparing $h$ and $g$.  

Final evaluation:  The paper over-claims its contributions and ignores some very related work (e.g. [Geifman & El-Yaniv, NeurIPS 2017]), thus necessitating substantial revisions to the text.  Moreover, the $g(x)$ selection function has not been demonstrated to behave as the core motivation for the work implies it should---namely, modeling $p(d_{\text{in}} | x)$.
